title: CHAPTER 17: SOCIO-RELIGIOUS REFORM MOVEMENTS IN INDIA

blocks.content: 1. Introduction: Background of Reform Movements

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Socio-religious reform movements emerged in the 19th and early 20th centuries to challenge caste discrimination, sati, child marriage, and denial of women's education.
Raja Rammohan Roy, known as the 'Father of Indian Renaissance', founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828 and brought about the abolition of sati in 1829.
Swami Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875, emphasizing the supreme authority of the Vedas and introducing the Shuddhi movement.
Swami Vivekananda represented Indian culture at the Parliament of Religions in 1893 and established the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan spearheaded the Aligarh Movement to advance modern education among Muslims, founding the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College.

blocks.content: The socio-religious reform movements of the 19th and early 20th centuries emerged as a response to the deep social, religious, and cultural stagnation present in Indian society. Indian society was affected by practices such as caste discrimination, untouchability, sati, child marriage, female infanticide, purdah system, and denial of education to women. At the same time, the impact of Western education, ideas of rationalism, humanism, liberty, equality, and the influence of the British legal system encouraged Indians to question traditional practices. These reform movements aimed not only at social upliftment but also laid the foundation of modern Indian nationalism.
2. Factors Responsible for the Rise of Reform Movements
Several factors contributed to the rise of socio-religious reform movements in India:

• Impact of Western education and English language
• Influence of Christian missionaries and criticism of Indian society
• Social evils and rigid religious practices
• Emergence of an educated Indian middle class
• Print media and spread of ideas
• Economic and political decline of traditional institutions
3. Brahmo Samaj (1828)

The Brahmo Samaj was founded in 1828 by Raja Rammohan Roy. It was one of the earliest socio-religious reform movements in India. The Brahmo Samaj aimed at reforming Hindu society by removing blind faith, idol worship, and social evils.
3.1 Teachings of Brahmo Samaj

• Belief in one God
• Opposition to idol worship
• Emphasis on reason and rational thinking
• Opposition to caste discrimination
• Support for widow remarriage and women’s education
3.2 Role of Raja Rammohan Roy
Raja Rammohan Roy is known as the ‘Father of Indian Renaissance’. He fought against social evils like sati and child marriage. His efforts led to the abolition of sati through the regulation of 1829.
4. Young Bengal Movement
Led by Henry Louis Vivian Derozio, the Young Bengal Movement promoted radical ideas, rationalism, freedom of thought, and questioned orthodox traditions.
These reform movements aimed not only at social upliftment but also laid the foundation of modern Indian nationalism.
5. Prarthana Samaj
Founded in Bombay, the Prarthana Samaj worked for social reforms such as widow remarriage, women’s education, and removal of caste restrictions.
6. Arya Samaj (1875)
The Arya Samaj was founded by Swami Dayanand Saraswati in 1875. It advocated a return to the Vedas and rejected idol worship.
6.1 Teachings of Arya Samaj

• Belief in Vedas as supreme authority
• Opposition to idol worship
• Promotion of education through DAV institutions
• Support for widow remarriage
• Shuddhi movement for reconversion
7. Ramakrishna Mission (1897)
The Ramakrishna Mission was founded by Swami Vivekananda in 1897. It emphasized practical spirituality and service to humanity.

rows: Belief in one God, opposition to idol worship, emphasis on reason and rational thinking
Return to Vedas as supreme authority, rejection of idol worship, Shuddhi movement
Practical spirituality, service to humanity, global promotion of Indian philosophy

blocks.content: 7.1 Swami Vivekananda
Swami Vivekananda popularized Indian philosophy worldwide. His speech at the Parliament of Religions (1893) brought global recognition to Indian culture.
8. Muslim Reform Movements
Muslim reform movements aimed at removing social stagnation and promoting modern education.
8.1 Aligarh Movement
Led by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, the Aligarh Movement emphasized modern education. The Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College later became Aligarh Muslim University.
9. Sikh Reform Movements
The Singh Sabha Movement aimed at purifying Sikh religion and promoting education.
10. Women Reform Movements

items: Abolition of Sati (1829): Brought into effect through regulations advocated by Raja Rammohan Roy.
Founders & Movements: Brahmo Samaj (Raja Rammohan Roy, 1828), Arya Samaj (Swami Dayanand Saraswati, 1875), Ramakrishna Mission (Swami Vivekananda, 1897).
Aligarh Movement: Led by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan; established the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (later Aligarh Muslim University).
Parliament of Religions (1893): Swami Vivekananda delivered his landmark speech popularizing Indian philosophy globally.

blocks.content: Reformers like Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar worked for widow remarriage and women’s education.
11. Impact and Significance of Reform Movements
Socio-religious reform movements weakened rigid traditions, promoted social equality, and prepared the ground for Indian nationalism.
12. Limitations of Reform Movements
These movements were largely confined to urban areas and educated classes. They did not fully reach the masses.
